summary: Sambro Island Light, at the mouth of Halifax Harbour, was voted by Nova Scotia's first assembly in 1758 and is called North America's oldest operating lighthouse; its tower was raised in 1906.

lens.where: Maritime Museum of the Atlantic, Halifax (1906-1966 lens)

access.note: Island reached by boat only; Coast Guard property. Trips are offered only occasionally (Nova Scotia Lighthouse Preservation Society).

events.note: Lottery proposed to pay for a light on 'Cape Sambrough'; failed
Act of 2 October 1758 (first session of the Nova Scotia assembly) voted £1,000 for a lighthouse; work begun by early November
Letter dated Halifax 28 April 1759 says the light was lighted on the 23rd; Joseph Rous hired as first keeper 25 April 1759
Sloop Granby lost on ledges near the island, 8 April 1771; inquiry into the keeper and the light follows
Matthew Pennell in charge; fountain lamps with flues installed
Commission reports on the light; lantern of 128 small panes, wooden sashes; artillery guard stationed
New iron lantern with plate-glass windows (the Society: 1864; Lighthouse Friends: 1865)
Daboll trumpet with caloric engine, 20 September 1865
Steam fog whistle started 16 October 1876
Second-order Fresnel lens by Chance Brothers, $4,942
Steamer Daniel Steinmann lost on the ledges north-east of the island, night of 3 April 1884; nine saved
Gilkie household lit the shore to guide a ship's boat in (seven men) and Stewart and three others put out at daybreak to take two men from the rigging
Steam whistle discontinued 15 June 1891; explosive (bomb rocket) signal every 20 minutes, every 10 from 1899
First-order Fresnel flashing light (Barbier, Benard & Turenne, Paris) replaces second-order fixed light; tower raised 20 ft with concrete, finished November 1906, $2,934
Tower repainted with white and red bands for visibility against snow
SS City of Sydney struck Sambro ledges in dense fog, 17 March 1914; total loss (the casualty return and inquiry table say Shag rock; no lives lost; master censured)
Vessel (name illegible in OCR) stranded and lost near Sambro Island, 5 February 1917; all on board saved
City of Vienna stranded near Sister ledges, 2 July 1918
Bohemian stranded near Sisters Rock, Sambro ledges; six lives lost; inquiry 5-6 March 1920
National historic site designation with plaque in the village of Sambro (the Society's wording)
Tower found swaying in January; grouted and a concrete collar built round the base
Diaphone
First-order Fresnel lens replaced by a DCB-36 rotating beacon; lens lent to the Maritime Museum of the Atlantic
Aluminium lantern room replaces the 1906 lantern (Lighthouse Friends: May 1968; the Society's dated list and its 1998 repair notes also say 1968, though its narrative says 1966)
Last keeper left the island
Tower classified (gas house recognized) under the federal heritage buildings policy
Concrete deck and shingles repaired, August-December 1998
Storm surge in April tore out the submarine power cable
Solarized in March 2008: Tideland TRB400 lens system and electronic horns replace the DCB-36 and diaphone
Head keeper's house (1960s) lost to fire in September 2008
$1.3 million federal contract to restore the tower's stone structure and concrete foundation

keepers.name: Joseph Rous
keepers.note: First keeper; brother of the naval captain John Rous (DCB). Lighthouse Friends: hired 25 April 1759, died May 1769.

keepers.name: Joseph Woodmass
keepers.note: Appointed after Rous died (Lighthouse Friends); not in the Society's list.

keepers.name: Matthew Pennell, Sr.
keepers.note: Kept the light until his death in early 1801; petitioned for a pension in 1799 aged 85.

keepers.name: William Gilkie
keepers.note: The Society's list gives 1856-1875. Lighthouse Friends: died July 1875. Not named in Ryder's 1862 report; the lists put him in charge then.

keepers.name: Joseph Gilkie
keepers.note: Son of William; had run the fog trumpet; drowned 1 March 1876 trying to reach the island from the mainland (Lighthouse Friends).

keepers.name: Alfred Gilkie
keepers.note: Brother of Joseph. Lighthouse Friends: 1876-1915 (but also says 'nearly thirty years'). The Department of Marine staff tables list 'Gilkie, Henry A' at Sambro (1901 table: appointed 8 January 1877; 1906 table: month January only) and 'Alfred Gilkie' in the same position in the 1911 table.

keepers.name: Arthur J. Gilkie
keepers.note: Son of Alfred. Department table: appointed 19 April 1914, salary $880.

keepers.name: William A. Smith
keepers.note: Noticed the tower swaying in January 1950.

keepers.name: John G. Fairservice
keepers.note: Last keeper; left the island in 1988 (Lighthouse Friends). The Society's list gives 'Fairservice, J.G. 1968-19XX'.

keepers.name: Kelly Fairservice Brown
keepers.note: Listed by the Nova Scotia Lighthouse Preservation Society after J.G. Fairservice, 'Brown, Kelly Fairservice 19XX-1988'; start year not given.

keepers.name: James Skinner
keepers.note: Head engineer of the steam fog whistle; started it on 16 October 1876.

keepers.name: Alexander Gilkie
keepers.note: Assistant engineer from 1876 to 'at least 1881' (Lighthouse Friends); in 1884 he relieved the engineer on the fog whistle and gave the Indianapolis Journal's account of the Daniel Steinmann wreck (the page prints his name as 'Alex. Gilnie'; taken to be Alexander Gilkie because he calls the keeper 'my brother Alfred'). Brother of the keeper Alfred.

keepers.name: Alex. Houseman
keepers.note: Engineer in charge of the fog whistle in April 1884 (Indianapolis Journal).

keepers.name: Stewart Gilkie
keepers.note: Brother of the keeper Alfred; lived on the island in April 1884 and rowed out to the Daniel Steinmann's rigging at daybreak. Printed only as 'Stewart'; surname inferred from his being the speaker's brother.

wrecks.outcome: Struck ledges near the island in a storm; all aboard lost; carrying £3,000 for naval staff pay

wrecks.vessel: Daniel Steinmann (steamer, White Cross Line, Antwerp to Halifax and New York)
wrecks.outcome: Struck the ledges north-east of the island in fog and rain about 10 pm and sank 300-400 yards off; nine reported saved (captain, five sailors, three passengers): seven in a ship's boat guided in by lights lit by the Gilkie household, two taken from the rigging at daybreak by Stewart and three others (the captain counts three rescuers, another report five)

Struck Sambro ledges in dense fog (salvage report); the casualty return says 'struck off Shag rock, N.S.', total loss, no lives lost; full of water, cargo partly salved by the Cabot; master censured for an error of judgment (inquiry at Halifax 23-24 March 1914)

wrecks.vessel: Unnamed (name illegible in the OCR of the 1916-17 wreck return)
wrecks.outcome: Stranded and lost near Sambro Island; all on board saved; master severely censured for not sounding (inquiry at Halifax 12-13 February 1917)
Stranded near Sister ledges, Sambro; master not in fault but erred in not stopping on hearing the Sambro fog signal

Stranded near Sisters Rock, Sambro ledges (stranding day unreadable in the OCR); six lives lost; master Ernest C. Hiscoe at fault for not taking soundings, certificate suspended four months (inquiry at Halifax 5 and 6 March 1920; the day figure is OCR 'b', read as 6)

evidence.supports: oldest operating light; act of first session 1758
evidence.quote: Sambro Lighthouse is the oldest standing and operating lighthouse in the Americas. Legislation to establish the lighthouse was passed at the first session of the Legislative Assembly of Nova Scotia in 1758.

evidence.supports: location, shoals
evidence.quote: Sambro Island Lighthouse stands on a granite island about 2 nautical miles outside the entrance to Halifax Harbour, marking an area of dangerous shoals.

evidence.supports: Halifax founded 1749 as naval base; fog; thirty shoals
evidence.quote: Halifax was founded in 1749 as the major base for the British Navy in North America.

evidence.supports: entrance masked in fog; thirty shoals
evidence.quote: The entrance was, however, often masked in fog and the more than thirty shoals surrounding Sambro Island were a grave hazard.

evidence.supports: nothing marked the hazards for nine years
evidence.quote: For the first nine years after the founding of Halifax, no signal marked these hazards.

evidence.supports: 1752 lottery failed
evidence.quote: As early as 1752, the Governor and Council organized a lottery to cover the cost of building a light on "Cape Sambrough," but had no success.

evidence.supports: act of 2 October 1758, £1,000, vessel tax
evidence.quote: on the first day of the first session of the General Assembly of Nova Scotia, October 2, 1758, an act was passed to establish a lighthouse on "Sambro Outer Island." They appropriated 1,000 pounds from the duties paid on spirituous liquors, and instituted a tax on vessels entering the harbour.

evidence.supports: commissioners, work begun early November, temporary light
evidence.quote: Commissioners were appointed and matters were put quickly in hand. The site was chosen, the money voted, and by early November the work was begun. It is probable that a temporary light was established on the island.

evidence.supports: evidence light operational in 1759; Pennsylvania Gazette letter
evidence.quote: There is evidence that the new light was operational in 1759. The Pennsylvania Gazette, May 14, 1759, contains the following note as part of a letter from Halifax, dated April 28, 1759:

evidence.supports: lit 23 April 1759
evidence.quote: It was lighted the 23rd Instant; and as it is of Service to the Publick, to our Vessels as well as others

evidence.supports: position one league SW of the harbour
evidence.quote: It is situated one League S.W. of the Harbour, on Sambra Island.

evidence.supports: tower of stone, 60 ft to vane, light 115 ft
evidence.quote: The building was of stone, 60 feet high from the base to the weather vane crowning the lantern. The white fixed light was, thus, 115 feet above sea level.

evidence.supports: tower constructed 1758 or 1760
evidence.quote: The Sambro Island lighttower was constructed in 1758 or 1760.

evidence.supports: walls of cut granite 5 ft at base tapering to 4 ft
evidence.quote: The original portion of the tower is built of cut granite, five feet thick at the base and tapering to four feet where it joins the concrete extension added in 1906-07.

evidence.supports: 1834 lantern with 128 panes; commission; iron lantern 1864
evidence.quote: In 1834, the lantern had 128 small panes of glass that had to be kept clean. A Commission appointed in that year reported that nothing could be done to improve the light until a new iron lantern was installed. This was not done until 1864.

evidence.supports: cannons answered ships' signals in fog
evidence.quote: For many years Sambro was equipped with cannons to answer ship's signals in fog.

evidence.supports: 1906 raise: society says 22 feet; heritage review 20 feet
evidence.quote: In 1906, an extra 22 feet was added to the height of the tower.

evidence.supports: heritage review: raised 20 feet, 62 to 82 ft
evidence.quote: in 1906 the tower was raised 20 feet, changing its height from 62 to 82 feet.

evidence.supports: Pennell in charge 1772; fountain lamps with flues
evidence.quote: Nothing was done about this, for in 1772, Matthew Pennell was in charge of the light. At that time, fountain lamps with flues to carry off the smoke were installed. After that, there was far less trouble with the darkening of the glass which obscured the light.

evidence.supports: Gambier's report: accident for want of a light; ships fired at the lighthouse
evidence.quote: Commodore Gambier, Commander in Chief of the Naval Station, reported that "the fatal accident happened for want of a light being properly kept in the lighthouse." He noted that H. M. Ships had, on occasion, to fire at the lighthouse in order to make the keepers show a light.

evidence.supports: complaint about the cost of the light
evidence.quote: Other vessels complained at being forced to pay for a light which "is a great annual expense to the Government and serves no other purpose than the shameful one of putting money in the pockets of a nominee of the Governor's."

evidence.supports: inquiry: keeper appointed by governor, cheapest materials, fish oil
evidence.quote: An inquiry found that, indeed, the keeper was appointed by the Governor. He was allowed the duties paid by ships entering the port and procured only the cheapest materials. Fish oil fuelled the light and if it went out and no ships were in sight, it was left out.

evidence.supports: Gambier recommended government takeover
evidence.quote: Commodore Gambier recommended that the government take over operation of the Sambro Light.

evidence.supports: Granby of Boston wrecked 1771
evidence.quote: The wreck of the sloop Granby, of Boston, in 1771, with the loss of all hands, blew the situation wide open.

evidence.supports: 1950 tower swaying; 20 cm lean
evidence.quote: In January of 1950, lightkeeper W. A. Smith noticed that the lighthouse was swaying! It was found to be leaning by 20 centimeters.

evidence.supports: 1950 excavation: cracked mortar; grout and collar
evidence.quote: In the spring, excavations at the base discovered that the mortar was cracked and some stones were loose. In the fall, grout was pressure-pumped in and a concrete collar about 90 cm. thick and 2 m. high was installed to reinforce the base.

evidence.supports: 1966 lantern and beacon; diaphone 1963; electronic horns 2008
evidence.quote: In 1966 the classic iron lantern which crowned the tower was replaced with aluminium and a 36 inch airport beacon replaced the huge lens.

evidence.supports: fog signal sequence ending in 1963 diaphone
evidence.quote: Later, a steam fog horn was installed, then bomb rockets, after that acetylene guns, and finally, in 1963, a diaphone. In 2008 the diaphone was replaced by electonic horns.

evidence.supports: 1937 national historic site and plaque
evidence.quote: In 1937 Sambro Lighthouse was designated a National Historic Site and a plaque placed in the village of Sambro.

evidence.supports: 1996 Classified status
evidence.quote: In 1996 the lighthouse received Federal Heritage Review Board Classified status, the highest ranking status for Canadian Government Heritage Buildings.

evidence.supports: tower Classified, gas house Recognized
evidence.quote: Sambro Island Lighttower (Classified) Sambro Island Gas House (Recognized)

evidence.supports: 1998 repair started end of August; salt in the 1906 concrete
evidence.quote: Work began at the end of August 1998. The concrete platform was chipped away. It was discovered that the 1906 concrete mix used beach sand and stones (a common situation) and the resulting salt in the concrete had caused the deterioration.

evidence.supports: great chunks of concrete falling
evidence.quote: Great chunks of concrete were falling off.

evidence.supports: tower originally whitewashed; completed December 1998
evidence.quote: it could be seen that the tower was originally whitewashed.

evidence.supports: restoration completed December 1998
evidence.quote: The restoration work on the tower was completed in December, 1998

evidence.supports: solarized March 2008
evidence.quote: Sambro Lighthouse was successfully solarized with a powerful new lens and light in March 2008.

evidence.supports: painted 2008 ahead of 250th birthday
evidence.quote: Coast Guard is anxious that the lighthouse be in good shape for her 250th birthday in October 2008.

evidence.supports: owner and operator
evidence.quote: Owned by the Government of Canada Operated by the Canadian Coast Guard

evidence.supports: 1752 lottery scheme refunded
evidence.quote: The plan was to sell 1,000 tickets for 3£ each and retain fifteen percent of the 3,000£ that would be paid out to 200 winning tickets. When an insufficient number of tickets were sold, those that had purchased a ticket received a refund.

evidence.supports: lottery to raise £450
evidence.quote: a lottery was proposed to raise 450£ for the construction of a lighthouse on Sambro Island

evidence.supports: Captain Rous deeded the island
evidence.quote: an octagonal, stone tower was built on Sambro Island, which Captain Rous had deeded to the government.

evidence.supports: tower base 20 ft diameter, walls 5.5 ft
evidence.quote: At its base, the tower has a diameter of twenty feet, and its walls are five-and-half-feet thick.

evidence.supports: Joseph Rous hired 25 April 1759
evidence.quote: Joseph Rous, the brother of Captain Rous, was hired as the light

evidence.supports: Rous died May 1769; Woodmass appointed
evidence.quote: After Joseph Rous died in May 1769, Joseph Woodmass was appointed keeper of the lighthouse.

evidence.supports: Granby 8 April 1771
evidence.quote: On April 8, 1771, the sloop Granby struck ledges near Sambro Island during a storm and was dashed to pieces. The ship was carrying 3,000£ for payment of the naval staff at Halifax, and all aboard perished.

evidence.supports: naval captains obliged to fire at the lighthouse
evidence.quote: frequently obliged to fire at the lighthouse to make them shew a light.

evidence.supports: Pennell appointed 1772
evidence.quote: Matthew Pennell was appointed keeper of Sambro Island Lighthouse in 1772

evidence.supports: Pennell's 1799 petition
evidence.quote: In 1799, Keeper Pennell, who was then eighty-five, petitioned the government for a pension as he had been unable to save any money as keeper while raising four children and three orphaned grandchildren.

evidence.supports: Pennell granted 100£; died 1801; son appointed
evidence.quote: Keeper Pennell continued to serve as keeper until his death in early 1801, following which his son, Matthew Pennel, Jr., was appointed keeper.

evidence.supports: 1834 commissioners: complaints more than any other light
evidence.quote: In 1834, the Commissioners of Lighthouses of Nova Scotia noted that mariners complained of Sambro Island Lighthouse more than any other light in the province.

evidence.supports: 1834 commissioners: busiest harbour; defects conceded
evidence.quote: While they believed this was because it was located at the busiest harbor and thus passed by more vessels, the commissioners conceded that the lighthouse did have some defects.

evidence.supports: 1834 wooden lantern posts and sashes blocked the light
evidence.quote: Most notable was its wooden lantern room whose eight corner posts, which were nearly a foot square, and large wooden sashes blocked a good portion of the light.

evidence.supports: 1834 artillery guard
evidence.quote: An artillery guard was also stationed on the island by this time in order to fire cannons in response to the signal of vessels during periods of limited visibility.

evidence.supports: Ryder inspection 1862 at Milne's request
evidence.quote: In 1862, Alfred P. Ryder, Captain of the H.M.S. Hero inspected the lighthouse on Sambro Island at the request of Vice Admiral Alexander Milne.

evidence.supports: Ryder: lamps and reflectors
evidence.quote: There are 13 lamps, of which 9 have reflectors arranged round the edge of a flat and nearly circular table.

evidence.supports: Ryder: 128 panes
evidence.quote: if the number of panes of glass was a merit in a Light House, Sambro would probably stand at the head of the list of known Light Houses. It contains 128 small panes of glass.

evidence.supports: Ryder: keeper tilts lamps; oil swells with heat
evidence.quote: the keeper takes very good care that they shall not, for he invariably and intentionally places them out of adjustment every night

evidence.supports: Ryder: reason for tilting; keeper's words
evidence.quote: This is done to prevent the oil running over, when, as the keeper describes it, "it swells with the heat."

evidence.supports: Ryder: wedges of wood
evidence.quote: They were wedged back by small pieces of wood of unequal size and variable thickness.

evidence.supports: Ryder: little silver left
evidence.quote: there was so little silver left on them (they were 47 years old), that it could make but little difference

evidence.supports: Ryder recommended Fresnel lens and new lantern room
evidence.quote: Captain Ryder recommended that a Fresnel lens and new lantern room be installed atop Sambro Island Lighthouse

evidence.supports: new lamps promptly installed; lantern 1865
evidence.quote: New lamps and reflectors were promptly installed at Sambro Lighthouse as a result of Captain Ryder

evidence.supports: improved lantern 1865
evidence.quote: an improved lantern room with reflectors imported from Great Britain were placed atop the tower in 1865.

evidence.supports: Daboll trumpet 20 Sept 1865
evidence.quote: A Daboll trumpet, operated by a caloric engine, was placed in operation on Sambro Island on September 20, 1865.

evidence.supports: Daboll trumpet failures 1870; guns
evidence.quote: On June 16, 1870, the machinery was in such bad order that the keeper had to turn the fly wheel by hand, and on July 25, 1870, the equipment had completely broken down.

evidence.supports: two 24-pounders answer ships' signals
evidence.quote: Mariners were notified that signals from ships would be answered by the discharge of two twenty four-pounders in quick succession until further notice.

evidence.supports: steam whistle costs and buildings
evidence.quote: Messrs. Fleming & Son of Saint John, New Brunswick provided a steam fog whistle for Sambro Island for $7,250

evidence.supports: evaporating house to condense fresh water
evidence.quote: An evaporating house was built on the south side of the small inlet that serves as a harbour for the island.

evidence.supports: evaporating house condensed fresh water from salt water
evidence.quote: served to condense fresh water from salt water.

evidence.supports: DCB-36 on display at the museum
evidence.quote: The DCB-36 is now also on display at the Maritime Museum of the Atlantic.

evidence.supports: Slocum took his departure from George's Island, Halifax harbour
evidence.quote: I set my flag and squared away, taking my departure from George's Island before dark to sail east of Sable Island.

evidence.supports: wharf and tramway for coal
evidence.quote: A wharf was also built in the inlet, and a tramway was constructed to deliver coal from the wharf to the whistle house.

evidence.supports: Skinner started whistle 16 Oct 1876; ten-second blast
evidence.quote: James Skinner was appointed engineer at the station, and he placed the steam fog whistle in operation on October 16, 1876. When needed, the whistle gave a ten-second blast each minute.

evidence.supports: Alfred replaced Joseph, who drowned 1 March 1876
evidence.quote: Alfred replaced his brother Joseph as keeper, after Joseph drowned on March 1, 1876 while trying to reach the island from the mainland.

evidence.supports: Joseph Gilkie ran the trumpet; replaced father William who died July 1875
evidence.quote: Joseph Gilkie had been in charge of the fog trumpet when it was in operation and replaced his father William as keeper of the light when he died in July 1875.

evidence.supports: Alfred longest-serving; Arthur J. took over
evidence.quote: Alfred Gilkie, the longest-serving keeper on Sambro Island, retired in 1915, after nearly thirty years as head keeper. Arthur J. Gilkie took over form his father Alfred and served until 1929.

evidence.supports: 1877 second-order lens
evidence.quote: a second-order Fresnel lens , provided by Chance Brothers of Birmingham England at a cost of $4,942, was installed atop the lighthouse.

evidence.supports: 1891 whistle replaced by bomb rocket every twenty minutes
evidence.quote: The whistle on Sambro Island was accordingly discontinued on June 15, 1891, and a bomb rocket, fired every twenty minutes, was established instead.

evidence.supports: magazine and derrick; 1899 every ten minutes
evidence.quote: The water tank in the old fog-whistle house was converted into a magazine for storing the gun cotton cartridges, and a derrick was erected for firing the cartridges. In 1899, the frequency of the firing of the cartridges was increased to every ten minutes.

evidence.supports: 1908 red bands
evidence.quote: In 1908, the tower was given three horizontal red bands to make it more conspicuous when snow was on the ground.

evidence.supports: 1950 swaying; over fifty inches out of plumb
evidence.quote: In January 1950, Keeper William Smith noticed that the tower was swaying. Measurements taken subsequently showed the tower to be over fifty inches out of plumb.

evidence.supports: 1966 DCB-36 replaced Fresnel lens; lens loaned to museum
evidence.quote: A revolving airport-style beacon (a DCB-36) replaced the first-order Fresnel lens atop Sambro Island Lighthouse in 1966. The lens was permanently loaned to the Maritime Museum of the Atlantic, and can be seen at the museum today.

evidence.supports: 1968 aluminium lantern; Fairservice last keeper left 1988
evidence.quote: In May 1968, an aluminum lantern room replaced the first-order, circular lantern room that had been installed along with the lens in 1906. John G. Fairservice, the last keeper, left the island in 1988.

evidence.supports: plywood over dwellings 1998; vandals
evidence.quote: volunteers from the Nova Scotia Lighthouse Preservation Society installed plywood over the two abandoned keeper’s dwellings to retard further deterioration. Vandals had already stripped the hardwood floors and stairs from the houses.

evidence.supports: 1998 repair; shingles replaced; deck repaired
evidence.quote: Cureggio General Contractors were hired in 1998 to refurbish the lighthouse.

evidence.supports: storm surge April 2007 tore out cable
evidence.quote: A strong storm surge in April 2007, tore out the submarine cable that supplied electricity to Sambro Island.

evidence.supports: generators until March 2008 solar; Tideland TRB400; electronic horns
evidence.quote: Diesel generators were used to power the light until an array of solar panels was installed on the island in March 2008. A Tideland TRB400 lens system replaced the DCB-36 at this time, while electronic horns replaced the diaphone fog signal, which had been in use since 1963.

evidence.supports: painted summer 2008 for 250th anniversary
evidence.quote: During the summer of 2008, Sambro Island Lighthouse was painted so it would look its best for its 250th anniversary.

evidence.supports: head keeper's dwelling lost to fire
evidence.quote: The color pictures at the top of this page were taken in late August 2008. Roughly two weeks later, the head keeper’s dwelling, which dated from the 1960s, was lost to fire.

evidence.supports: 2016 contract $1.3 million Quinan
evidence.quote: In 2016, the federal government awarded a $1.3 million dollar contract to Quinan Construction Company of Orillia, Ontario to restore the tower’s stone structure and its concrete foundation.

evidence.supports: visible from Chebucto Head and Crystal Crescent; NSLPS trips
evidence.quote: Sambro Island Lighthouse is visible in the distance from Chebucto Head and Crystal Crescent Beach Provincial Park. Trips to the lighthouse are occasionally offered by the Nova Scotia Lighthouse Preservation Society.

evidence.supports: lens at Maritime Museum of the Atlantic; DCB-36 on display
evidence.quote: The lens was permanently loaned to the Maritime Museum of the Atlantic, and can be seen at the museum today.

resolved_conflicts.explanation: The record gives 1758 (first lit) and 1759 (built). 1758 is the year of the Assembly's act (2 October) and the start of work. The earliest dated notice of the light in use is a Halifax letter of 28 April 1759 saying it was lighted on the 23rd; the Society thinks a temporary light was probably shown earlier. The federal heritage review dates the tower '1758 or 1760'. This file gives first_lit 1759 because that is the earliest dated evidence; 1758 for a temporary light is plausible but not dated by any source read.

The Coast Guard List of Lights gives the tower as 20.7 m. The 1907 departmental report gives the lighthouse as 82 feet (25 m) from base to vane, which the Society repeats as 25 m base to top. facts.structures uses 25.0 m (base to vane).
The department's report says a 20-foot concrete wall; the Society's heritage review says 20 feet (62 to 82 ft) while its history says 22 feet.

The Department of Marine tables name the Sambro head keeper 'Gilkie, Henry A' (appointed 8 January 1877) in the 1901 and 1906 reports and 'Alfred Gilkie' in the 1911 list (the 1912 report's appointment column shows an initials entry that reads 'H. H. Gilkio, Jan. 8' in the OCR, not cited here). Lighthouse Friends gives Alfred 1876-1915. Probably one man (Henry Alfred?), but no source read says so.

The Society's narrative says the iron lantern was replaced by aluminium in 1966 together with the lens, but its own dated list and its 1998 repair notes say 1968, as does Lighthouse Friends (May 1968). The story gives 1966 for the lens and 1968 for the lantern.
The Society says about 2 nautical miles outside the entrance; Lighthouse Friends' map note says about 8 km (5 miles) southwest of the entrance. Both are given in the story.
Lighthouse Friends says the 3,000 pounds were for the naval staff at Halifax; the Society says dockyard staff. Both are given in the story.

The 1913-14 salvage report says the steamer struck Sambro ledges on 17 March 1914; the same volume's casualty return and inquiry table say Shag rock, N.S. (the Coast Guard List of Lights places a Shag Rock light buoy at Sambro). Both are given in the story.

notes_for_editor: Medium confidence. The structure, dates of the 1906 reconstruction, the later wrecks and the 1914-20 keeper entries rest on Department of Marine and Fisheries annual reports (primary). The 18th- and 19th-century material (lottery, Gambier and the Granby, Ryder's 1862 report, the Gilkie family, the fog-signal sequence, 1950 lean, restorations) rests on the Nova Scotia Lighthouse Preservation Society and Lighthouse Friends only; neither cites its primary sources on the page, and the Society's page and Lighthouse Friends disagree on several dates (see resolved_conflicts). The corpus holds Canadian annual reports only from fiscal 1900, so nothing primary was available for 1759-1899 except the Pennsylvania Gazette letter (as quoted by the Society), the DCB entry on John Rous and Johnson's 1889 mention of the Sambro fog-gun. Lighthouse Friends says Alfred Gilkie served 'nearly thirty years' but its own dates (1876-1915) make it 39; the keepers table here uses the dates, not the phrase. Conflict on the fog signal today: the record says 'horn', and the Society and Lighthouse Friends say electronic horns replaced the diaphone in 2008, but the Coast Guard List of Lights entry no. 507 shows no audible signal. Check the current List. Flash period: the 1906 apparatus flashed every 5 s (departmental report) and the Society says the DCB-36 flashed every 5 s; the Coast Guard now lists Fl W 6s. Not used (Wikipedia leads only, no second source read): the privateer battles of 1780-82 and 1813, the 1942 and 1944 U-boat incidents, Hurricane Juan damage to the gas house in 2003, the Captain Highliner commercials, 2007 silencing of the fog horn, the first lit date of 3 November 1758, and the 1937 'National Historic Event' wording (the Society says 'National Historic Site'; the Parks Canada directory page could not be read by the text tool). Photos: Lighthouse Friends shows a Nova Scotia Archives photo (1901) and a Library and Archives Canada photo (1906 addition); licences not checked, so none are listed. People named after 1960 (Soltesz, Gwynn, Fairservice, Thomas, Kelly Fairservice Brown) appear only as the published lists give them, in their public role. Process: the search budget was exceeded (five websearch.py queries, not three) and the page-read budget was about met only because several reads failed (Parks Canada directory pages are script-rendered; the NYT 403; Hoosier State Chronicles and mshshistory.com unreadable); counting failures, about 16 reads. loc.gov was slow (shared queue, one 503) but not refused. The Daniel Steinmann account (3 April 1884) rests on two newspaper pages (New-York Tribune 5 April, Indianapolis Journal 7 April). The Indianapolis page names the keeper's brother as 'Alex. Gilnie' (OCR for Gilkie, as I read it); his brother 'Stewart' is taken to be Stewart Gilkie. The captain's statement says he never heard the fog whistle; Gilkie's says it was stopped at 8:45 and restarted at 9:45; the papers print both. The initial Tribune dispatch said the fog hid the light, but the captain's own statement says he saw it and took it for Chebucto. Fatalities are given variously in the papers (about 124 aboard in the Tribune, 130 lives lost in the New York agents' message). FACT-CHECK 2026-10-21: keeper names from the OCR'd Department of Marine tables were checked by column position: 1901 p.150 (Gilkie, Henry A / Sambro / Jan. 8, 1877 are the first entries of the name, station and appointed columns); 1915 p.72 (A. J. Gilkie / Sambro light and explosive fog-signal / April 19, 1914, $880 are the first entries; the second and third, J. H. Finlay and E. Smith, match Sambro Harbour and Sambro Inner Island); 1911 p.238 (Alfred Gilkie falls at the Sambro Light and Fog Alarm position once the Sable Island superintendent line is used as the anchor). The Bohemian inquiry date reads 'March 5 and b' in the OCR; 6 is a reading, not confirmed. A web-search snippet (NYT, 2 March 1920, not read and not cited) suggests the Bohemian struck on 1 March 1920, which fits the inquiry. The first Daniel Steinmann account names the speaker 'Alex. Gilnie' (see keepers note).
